title: SI Joint Pain: Diagnosis, Injection & Fusion

sections.title: Technique & Approach
sections.content:
## SI Joint Diagnostic and Therapeutic Injection Technique

### Intra-Articular SI Joint Injection

1. **Patient positioning**: Prone on fluoroscopy table
2. **Fluoroscopic guidance**: Use AP or oblique views to visualize the SI joint — the inferior aspect of the joint is the typical entry point
3. **Needle selection**: 22-25 gauge, 3.5-inch spinal needle
4. **Target**: Inferior aspect of the SI joint under fluoroscopy
5. **Joint entry**: Advance the needle into the joint, confirming position with contrast arthrogram
6. **Arthrogram**: Inject contrast to confirm intra-articular position — should see dye filling the joint space
7. **Diagnostic injection**: Small volume (1-2 mL) of local anesthetic to confirm SI joint as pain source
8. **Therapeutic injection**: Add corticosteroid (40-80 mg triamcinolone or 6-8 mg dexamethasone)

### Critical Point: Image Guidance Is Required

**Blind SI joint injections have extremely poor accuracy** — only 12-22% intra-articular placement rate without imaging guidance. Fluoroscopic (or CT/ultrasound) guidance is mandatory.

### IPSIS Fluoroscopic Technique Details

The IPSIS Technical Manual provides detailed guidance on achieving reliable SI joint access:

**Fluoroscopic Setup and Target Acquisition:**
- Apply 10-25 degrees of cephalad tilt so the inferior joint projects just above the superior pubic ramus; this separates posterior from anterior joint planes vertically
- Obtain an adjusted AP view (typically 5-20 degrees contralateral oblique) to superimpose the anterior and posterior joint margins at the caudal third
- Then rotate ipsilaterally to separate the joint lines horizontally — the medial silhouette usually represents the posterior (accessible) joint line
- Adjust obliquity until the inferior one-third of the medial joint line cortex is maximally crisp, indicating the beam is parallel to the posterior opening

**Needle Placement Strategy:**
- Target 1-2 cm cephalad to the inferior aspect of the joint
- Consider a slight medial-to-lateral trajectory given the typical joint orientation and unseen osteophytes
- Advance to sacral periosteum first (just medial to the joint line to prevent overpenetration), then redirect laterally into the joint
- Joint entry is recognized by loss of bony resistance followed by a subtle additional loss of resistance — the feeling of articular glide between opposing surfaces

**Arthrogram Interpretation:**
- The joint capacity is typically 2.0 mL or less — inject only 0.1-0.2 mL of contrast initially
- Initial intra-articular flow will cap the inferior aspect of the lucent joint space and fill a slightly expanded inferior recess
- True intra-articular spread appears as a thin line (<1 mm) centered between the cortical joint margins
- Normal sacculations may extend peripherally from the joint space
- If resistance to injection is encountered, rotate or slightly withdraw the needle (bevel may be in articular cartilage)
- Total injectate for diagnostic blocks should not exceed 1.5 mL; total volume (including contrast) should not exceed 2 mL

**Osteophyte Challenge:**
- Osteophytes typically arise from the iliac side, arcing lateral to medial over the inferior joint
- These are not visible on fluoroscopy because they are perpendicular to the X-ray beam, but they are readily apparent on CT
- A default medial-to-lateral needle trajectory may allow passage underneath unseen osteophytes
- Pre-procedure CT review is highly valuable for identifying these obstacles

**Capsular Defects and Extra-Articular Spread:**
- Capsular defects are present in 20-30% of patients; injectate may flow through ventral capsular foramina to the lumbosacral trunk or S1 foramen
- This extra-articular anesthetic spread can cause temporary leg numbness/weakness and compromises block specificity

### SI Joint Lateral Branch Blocks

This is a newer diagnostic/prognostic tool used before SI joint RFA:

1. **Target nerves**: Lateral branches of S1-S3 dorsal rami (and sometimes L5 dorsal ramus)
2. **Technique**: Small-volume local anesthetic blocks at each lateral branch target
3. **Fluoroscopic targets**: Along the lateral ala of the sacrum near the posterior sacral foramina
4. **Purpose**: Diagnose posterior SI joint complex pain and predict response to RFA

### IPSIS Sacral Lateral Branch Block (SLBB) Technique

The IPSIS manual distinguishes SLBBs from intra-articular SI joint blocks — they target different structures and answer different clinical questions:

**Anatomy of the Posterior Sacral Network (PSN):**
- The posterior SI joint complex (ligaments, posterior capsule, syndesmosis) is innervated by the PSN — a plexus formed by lateral branches of S1-3 plus variable contributions from L5 dorsal ramus and S4
- The PSN innervates the short and long posterior SI ligaments, interosseous SI ligaments, and part of the sacrotuberous ligament
- The middle cluneal nerves also arise from the PSN, providing cutaneous sensation to the medial buttock

**Critical Fluoroscopic Landmark — The Arcuate Line:**
- The perceived lateral margin of the sacral foramen on fluoroscopy is actually deep within the foramen (the true lateral margin is oblique to the X-ray beam and invisible)
- The inflection point of the arcuate line approximates the true anatomic center of the dorsal foramen
- All SLBB targets must be placed 8-10 mm lateral to this inflection point to avoid unintended foraminal needle placement

**Clockface Target Technique (multi-site, multi-depth):**
- Uses clockface coordinates around each dorsal sacral foramen, with targets 8-10 mm lateral to the arcuate line inflection:
  - S1: 6 and 7:30 (left) / 4:30 and 6 (right)
  - S2: 6:30, 8, and 9:30 (left) / 2:30, 4, and 5:30 (right)
  - S3: 9:30 and 11 (left) / 1 and 2:30 (right)
- At each target: inject 0.2 mL anesthetic on periosteum, withdraw one bevel-length, inject 0.2 mL more
- Validated multi-site, multi-depth approach produces reliable anesthesia of the dorsal SI joint complex (single-site, single-depth blocks were shown to be inadequate)

**Palisade Technique (alternative):**
- Six or more needles placed no more than 1 cm apart along a straight line 8-10 mm lateral to the arcuate line
- Spans from just above the S1 foramen to the mid-lower margin of S3 (or S4)
- Creates a continuous strip of anesthesia covering all pertinent lateral branches

**Confirming a Successful Block:**
- A technically adequate SLBB should produce hypoesthesia (numbness) of the medial buttock skin in the middle cluneal nerve distribution
- This is a useful bedside check to confirm the block reached the intended targets
- The L5 dorsal ramus must also be blocked to ensure complete posterior SI joint complex anesthesia

### SI Joint RFA Technique

- **Technology**: Cooled RF is preferred over conventional RF for SI joint ablation
- **Multiple electrodes**: Required to cover the variable course of the lateral branches
- **Targets**: S1-S3 lateral branches along the sacrum
- **Limitation**: RFA only addresses **posterior innervation** — the anterior SI joint (innervated by L2-S2 ventral rami) remains innervated

### IPSIS SLBRFN (Sacral Lateral Branch Radiofrequency Neurotomy) Details

The IPSIS manual describes two primary RF approaches for SI joint denervation:

**Clockface Technique (large-lesion monopolar/cooled RF):**
- Uses the same clockface targets as the SLBB technique (8-10 mm lateral to arcuate line inflection)
- Large-gauge cannulae (16-18G) with 10 mm active tips, or 17G internally cooled RF probes
- Cooled RF generator set to 60 degrees C, but intralesional temperature reaches 80 degrees C for 150 seconds
- Conventional monopolar lesions at 80-85 degrees C for 180 seconds at each target
- All clockface targets at each foramen must be lesioned for proper denervation

**Palisade Technique (bipolar RF strip lesioning):**
- Six or more parallel large-gauge cannulae placed no more than 1 cm apart
- Bipolar lesioning between adjacent cannulae creates a continuous coagulation strip
- Avoids the bow-tie effect (diminished lesion in the center between electrodes)
- 80-85 degrees C for 180 seconds; some practitioners use higher temperatures (up to 90 degrees C) or longer times

**Safety Note — Foraminal Cannula Placement:**
- The same fluoroscopic illusion that affects SLBBs applies to RFN: the perceived lateral foraminal margin is deep within the foramen
- RF lesioning within the foramen can injure the ventral ramus
- Cannulae that appear to project deep on lateral imaging may actually be correctly placed on the curved dorsal sacral surface

**L5 Dorsal Ramus RFN:**
- Should be performed concurrently for complete posterior SI joint complex denervation

### Percutaneous SI Joint Fusion

- **iFuse (SI-BONE)**: Triangular titanium implants placed percutaneously across the SI joint under fluoroscopic guidance
- **Approach**: Lateral approach through the ilium into the sacrum
- **Competitors**: Multiple companies now offer various designs — screws, implants, allograft options
- Some newer devices come in from posterior, and companies differentiate themselves with terms like "stabilize" or "distract" rather than "fuse"
keyPoints: Blind SI joint injections have only 12-22% accuracy — image guidance is mandatory
The inferior aspect of the SI joint is the standard entry point under fluoroscopy
IPSIS technique: 10-25 degrees cephalad tilt, then contralateral oblique to superimpose joint margins, then ipsilateral oblique to separate and target the posterior (medial) joint line
Joint capacity is typically 2 mL or less — inject only 0.1-0.2 mL contrast initially; total diagnostic injectate should not exceed 1.5 mL
Osteophytes are invisible on fluoroscopy (perpendicular to beam) but visible on CT — a medial-to-lateral trajectory can pass underneath them
Capsular defects in 20-30% of patients allow extra-articular spread to the lumbosacral trunk/S1 foramen, compromising block specificity
SLBB targets must be 8-10 mm lateral to the arcuate line inflection point — the perceived fluoroscopic foraminal margin is actually deep within the foramen
Clockface targets for SLBBs/SLBRFN: S1 (6/7:30 left, 4:30/6 right), S2 (6:30/8/9:30 left, 2:30/4/5:30 right), S3 (9:30/11 left, 1/2:30 right)
Multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs are required — single-site, single-depth blocks were shown to be inadequate for reliable anesthesia
A technically successful SLBB should produce medial buttock hypoesthesia (middle cluneal nerve distribution)
Lateral branch blocks of S1-S3 are the diagnostic tool before SI joint RFA (analogous to MBBs for facet RFA)
SI joint RFA only addresses posterior innervation — anterior innervation remains intact
Cooled RF is preferred over conventional RF for SI joint ablation due to variable nerve anatomy
L5 dorsal ramus RFN must be performed concurrently with SLBRFN for complete posterior SI joint complex denervation
Percutaneous SI fusion uses triangular titanium implants placed through the ilium into the sacrum
Multiple competing SI fusion devices now exist with various approaches and terminology

sections.title: Clinical Decision-Making
sections.content:
## Diagnosing SI Joint Pain

### The Fortin Finger Test

This is the first screening tool for SI joint pain:
- Ask the patient to point with one finger to the area of maximal pain
- **Positive**: Patient localizes pain to the area immediately inferomedial to the PSIS (within one fingerbreadth)
- **Sensitivity**: ~100% — if patients point elsewhere, SI joint pain is unlikely
- **Specificity**: Lower (~50-60%) — other structures nearby can cause similar localization
- **Key principle**: A negative Fortin test effectively **rules out** SI joint pain as a primary diagnosis

### Pain Referral Pattern

- Typically refers to the **buttock, posterior thigh (above the knee), and groin**
- Can mimic L5/S1 radiculopathy
- Rarely refers below the knee
- Groin pain component is more specific for SI joint origin
- Usually unilateral but can be bilateral
- **Important**: SI joint pain does NOT typically radiate UP into the lumbar spine

### Physical Examination Provocative Tests

Multiple provocation tests should be performed; **3 or more positive tests** increases diagnostic accuracy significantly:

- **Distraction test**: Anterior gapping force on ASISs
- **Compression test**: Lateral compression on iliac crests
- **Thigh thrust**: Hip flexed to 90 degrees, axial load through femur
- **Gaenslen test**: One hip extended off table edge, other flexed
- **FABER (Patrick) test**: Flexion, ABduction, External Rotation
- **Sacral thrust**: Posterior-to-anterior force on sacrum

**Laslett M et al. (2005)**: 3+ positive provocation tests have **sensitivity of ~94%** for SI joint pain confirmed by diagnostic injection.

### Diagnostic Injection Protocol

Similar to the facet pain paradigm:
1. **First injection**: Intra-articular with local anesthetic under fluoroscopy
2. **Positive response**: >75% pain relief confirms SI joint as pain source
3. **Confirmatory injection**: Second block with different anesthetic for increased specificity
4. **SIS recommends controlled blocks** before proceeding to advanced interventions

### IPSIS Distinction: Intra-Articular Blocks vs. Lateral Branch Blocks

This is a critical conceptual distinction emphasized in the IPSIS manual:

- **Intra-articular SI joint blocks** diagnose pain arising from the synovial joint itself (innervated predominantly by L2-S2 ventral rami anteriorly, with lesser dorsal contribution from S1-3 lateral branches)
- **Sacral lateral branch blocks (SLBBs)** diagnose pain from the posterior SI joint complex (ligaments, posterior capsule, syndesmosis), which is innervated by the posterior sacral network
- These are **not interchangeable** — positive SLBBs predict response to SLBRFN, while intra-articular blocks do not reliably predict RFA success
- Dual SLBBs with significant relief (50% or 80% threshold, depending on protocol) are generally considered necessary before proceeding to SLBRFN
- The distinction between intra-articular and posterior SI joint complex pain has important treatment implications

### SI Joint Is Overdiagnosed

Everything in the lower lumbar spine refers pain to the buttock — L4-5 disc problems, L5-S1 pathology, facet joints, SI joint. The SI joint is frequently blamed when the true pain generator is elsewhere. Proper diagnostic workup is essential.

### Do Not Forget Sacral Insufficiency Fractures

In elderly patients (especially osteoporotic postmenopausal women), always consider sacral insufficiency fractures:
- Present identically to SI joint pain
- Diagnosed by MRI (STIR sequence) or CT — fracture lines in sacral ala
- Treatment: Rest, analgesics, osteoporosis management
- Will NOT respond to SI joint injection
keyPoints: Negative Fortin finger test effectively rules out SI joint pain as the primary diagnosis
3+ positive provocation tests yield 94% sensitivity for SI joint pain (Laslett 2005)
SI joint pain does NOT typically radiate up into the lumbar spine — pain should be below L5
SI joint is frequently overdiagnosed — everything in the lower lumbar spine refers to the buttock
Always consider sacral insufficiency fractures in elderly osteoporotic patients with acute SI region pain
Blind SI joint injections are inaccurate (12-22%) — image guidance is mandatory
Controlled diagnostic blocks are recommended before advanced interventions (RFA or fusion)
IPSIS emphasizes that intra-articular blocks and SLBBs target different structures — they are not interchangeable for patient selection
The SI joint receives dominant ventral innervation from L2-S2 ventral rami anteriorly, with lesser dorsal innervation from S1-3 lateral branches
Dual SLBBs with significant pain relief are generally required before proceeding to SLBRFN

sections.title: Evidence & Guidelines
sections.content:
## Diagnostic Evidence

### Fortin JD & Falco FJ (1997) — Spine

Established the Fortin finger test by studying asymptomatic volunteers with provocative SI joint distension:
- Mapped pain referral patterns from the SI joint
- Pain was predominantly over the PSIS
- ~33% had referral toward the greater trochanter and proximal thigh
- Established the anatomical basis for the Fortin finger test

### Laslett M et al. (2005) — Spine

Demonstrated the composite diagnostic value of provocation tests:
- **3+ positive tests**: Sensitivity of ~94% for SI joint pain confirmed by diagnostic injection
- Individual tests have variable sensitivity and specificity
- The composite approach is significantly more reliable than any single test

## SI Joint RFA Evidence (Equivocal)

The evidence for SI joint RFA is **more mixed than for facet RFA** — an important teaching point:

- **Patel N et al. (2012)** — Pain Medicine: RCT showing significant improvement with **cooled RFA vs sham** at 3 months. One of the few positive RCTs.
- **Cohen SP et al. (2008)**: Inconsistent results with conventional (non-cooled) RFA

**Reasons for equivocal evidence**:
1. **Variable innervation**: The SI joint has complex, variable innervation patterns between individuals
2. **Large joint**: Multiple sources of innervation (anterior via L2-S2 ventral rami; posterior via S1-S3 lateral branches)
3. **Posterior denervation only**: RFA addresses only posterior innervation
4. **Technical challenges**: Placing multiple electrodes along variable lateral branch courses
5. **Selection issues**: Studies using intra-articular blocks to select for lateral branch RFA have a mismatch

### IPSIS Anatomical Studies on Lateral Branch Targets

Key cadaveric and anatomical studies referenced in the IPSIS manual have refined the procedural targets:

- **Dreyfuss et al. (2008)**: Demonstrated that single-site, single-depth sacral lateral branch blocks failed to reliably anesthetize the posterior SI joint complex
- **Dreyfuss et al. (2009)**: Showed that multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs using 0.2 mL at each target with periosteal and superficial deposits consistently achieved reliable posterior SI complex anesthesia
- **Stout et al. (2018)**: Dissected 40 additional joints to determine more precise lateral branch locations, refining the clockface SLBB/SLBRFN targets used in current IPSIS guidelines
- **Roberts (2021)**: Provided detailed SI joint innervation anatomy showing the posterior sacral network and its consistent contributions from S1-3 lateral branches
- **Cosman (2011)**: Described the bipolar palisade RF strip lesion geometry and its implications for achieving complete lateral branch coagulation

## SI Joint Fusion Evidence

### INSITE Trial — Polly DW et al. (2015) — Annals of Surgery

Prospective multicenter RCT comparing SI joint fusion (iFuse) to non-surgical management:
- Significantly superior outcomes for fusion in **VAS pain, ODI disability, and quality of life** at 6 months
- Crossover design allowed non-surgical patients to receive fusion

### Additional Fusion Studies

- **SALLY (Dengler J et al., 2019)**: Prospective multicenter study showing durable 2-year outcomes
- **iMIA Trial (Duhon BS et al., 2016)**: European RCT confirming superiority over conservative management
- **Long-term data**: 4-5 year follow-up studies showing maintained improvement

### Medicare Coverage Criteria for SI Fusion

1. SI joint pain confirmed by at least 1-2 positive diagnostic injections
2. Pain duration of at least 6 months
3. Failure of at least 6 months of conservative management
4. Baseline NRS pain >5/10
5. Positive provocative examination tests
6. Absence of generalized pain disorder as primary diagnosis

## UpToDate: SI Joint Glucocorticoid Injection Evidence

UpToDate provides a sobering assessment of the evidence for SI joint glucocorticoid injections:

### Randomized Trial Data

- Only **three small RCTs** exist, enrolling a combined total of just **54 patients**
- Both intra-articular and periarticular steroid injections showed **short-term benefits** for SI joint pain in these trials
- A subsequent multicenter comparative-effectiveness study demonstrated some intermediate-term benefits, but these improvements **did not achieve the minimum clinically important difference (MCID)**
- UpToDate recommends glucocorticoid injections for chronic, severe SI joint pain with a **Grade 2C** (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence)

### Clinical Significance

This limited evidence base supports Dr. O'Brien's clinical teaching that intra-articular SI joint injections are primarily diagnostic rather than therapeutic. The failure to reach MCID in a multicenter study reinforces that steroid injections alone are unlikely to provide meaningful long-term relief for most SI joint pain patients.

## UpToDate: SI Joint RFA Evidence

UpToDate synthesizes the RFA evidence for SI joint pain:

### Cooled RFA Trials

- A small randomized trial of cooled RFA targeting the primary dorsal rami and sacral lateral branch nerves (L4-L5) demonstrated **50% improvement in pain scores compared with placebo at 6-month follow-up**
- A multicenter randomized trial of 210 patients with SI joint pain (confirmed by positive injection response) showed cooled RFA produced **modestly improved pain, disability, and quality-of-life scores** compared with standard medical management (pharmacotherapy, injections, integrative therapies) through 12-month follow-up

### Combined Joint Disease RFA Trials

- A subsequent series of parallel RCTs studied patients with facet disease, SI joint disease, or combined facet/SI/disc disease
- The addition of radiofrequency denervation **did not produce clinically meaningful improvement** compared with a standardized exercise program alone
- However, the SI joint and combined disease subgroups **did show modest pain improvement** with interventional treatment, even though the overall result was negative

### UpToDate Recommendation

- For refractory pain from presumed SI joint etiology, UpToDate suggests RFA with a **Grade 2C** recommendation
- They acknowledge the evidence is limited by inconsistent trial results and study heterogeneity
- Glucocorticoid injections are considered a reasonable alternative for SI joint pain

### Cooled RF Rationale

- Cooled RFA circulates cool water through the probe tip, creating a slightly larger lesion than conventional RFA
- This larger lesion size provides theoretical benefit for conditions where target nerve location varies between individuals — which is precisely the challenge with the sacral lateral branches
- This aligns with the IPSIS teaching that cooled RF is preferred for SI joint denervation
keyPoints: Fortin (1997): Established SI joint pain referral patterns and the finger test from volunteer distension studies
Laslett (2005): 3+ positive provocation tests yield 94% sensitivity for SI joint pain
SI joint RFA evidence is equivocal — variable innervation and anterior/posterior mismatch are key issues
Patel (2012): Cooled RFA showed benefit over sham — most positive studies use cooled technology
INSITE Trial (Polly 2015): RCT showing SI fusion superior to conservative management
Medicare requires 6+ months of pain, failed conservative care, and positive diagnostic injections for fusion coverage
Industry sponsorship of SI fusion studies warrants critical appraisal of the evidence
Dreyfuss (2008/2009): Single-site SLBBs are inadequate; multi-site, multi-depth technique produces reliable posterior SI complex anesthesia
Stout (2018): Refined clockface SLBB/SLBRFN targets based on cadaveric dissections of 40 additional SI joints
Roberts (2021): Mapped the posterior sacral network anatomy showing consistent S1-3 lateral branch contributions
UpToDate: Only 3 small RCTs (54 total patients) support SI joint glucocorticoid injections — short-term benefit only
UpToDate: A multicenter comparative-effectiveness study of SI joint steroid injections showed benefit that did not reach the MCID
UpToDate: Cooled RFA showed 50% pain improvement vs placebo at 6 months in a small RCT
UpToDate: A 210-patient multicenter RCT of cooled RFA showed modest improvement in pain, disability, and QoL through 12 months vs standard medical management
UpToDate: Parallel RCTs adding RFA to exercise did not achieve clinically meaningful improvement overall, though SI joint and combined disease subgroups showed modest benefit
UpToDate recommends RFA (Grade 2C) for refractory SI joint pain, acknowledging limited and inconsistent evidence
UpToDate: Cooled RF creates larger lesions than conventional RF — advantageous when target nerve location varies (as with sacral lateral branches)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (Dr. O'Brien)
sections.content:
## Dr. O'Brien on SI Joint Pain

### SI Joint Is Way Overdiagnosed

Dr. O'Brien is direct about this point: the SI joint is way overdiagnosed. The reason is that everything in the lower lumbar spine — L4-5 disc problems, L5-S1 pathology, facet joints — all refer pain to the buttock. So when a patient presents with buttock pain, the SI joint gets blamed when the true generator is often elsewhere.

His screening criterion is practical: SI joint pain should be **below the lumbar spine** — predominantly buttock and referred hip area. If the patient has significant lumbar pain, think about other generators first.

### The Fortin Finger Test in Practice

Dr. O'Brien references Joe Fortin's work directly. Fortin took asymptomatic volunteers, put contrast into their SI joints, distended the capsule, and mapped the pain patterns. Almost everyone's pain was right over the PSIS, with about a third radiating toward the greater trochanter and a little into the thigh. Usually it does not go down the whole leg, though there are always exceptions.

Dr. O'Brien published what he believes is the only MRI arthrogram of the SI joint, from a patient around 2001 who had a ventral tear of her joint. She had radicular-type pain along with SI tenderness, and when he got medicine into the joint, it was the first time her pain had ever completely resolved.

### SI Injections Are More Diagnostic Than Therapeutic

Dr. O'Brien views intra-articular SI joint injections as primarily diagnostic, not therapeutic. Unless the patient has true inflammation of the joint (such as a spondyloarthropathy), the therapeutic benefit is limited. Having patients come back every three or four months for SI injections for the rest of their life does not make sense.

### The RFA Evidence Problem

Dr. O'Brien notes that SI joint RFA evidence is probably equivocal because the studies were based on patients selected using intra-articular injections, but that is not how you select for RFA of the joint. You need to do lateral branch blocks to diagnose SI joint complex pain that would justify doing an RFA. The mismatch between diagnostic method and treatment target is a fundamental problem with the existing literature.

He also notes that the SI joint is innervated both ventrally and posteriorly, so RFA of the posterior lateral branches does not address the entire joint.

### Sacral Insufficiency Fractures

Dr. O'Brien emphasizes that especially in osteoporotic women over 70, he does not hesitate to get an MRI. Sacral insufficiency fractures look just like SI pain — everything hurts in the same location. You need to rule them out because they will not respond to SI joint injection.

### Industry Skepticism for SI Fusion

Dr. O'Brien observes that once an indication is established for SI joint treatment, many companies emerge to profit from it. He notes over 20 companies now offer percutaneous SI joint fusion devices. He is cautious about industry-sponsored studies, noting that study sites with negative results may not get invited back. Most of his patients, even when confirmed as having SI joint pain, do not want to undergo fusion — they have to be quite debilitated to pursue it.
keyPoints: SI joint is way overdiagnosed — all lower lumbar pathology refers to the buttock
SI joint pain should be below the lumbar spine: buttock and hip area, not lumbar
Intra-articular SI injections are more diagnostic than therapeutic in most cases
SI joint RFA studies are equivocal partly because patient selection used intra-articular blocks, not lateral branch blocks
Always get MRI in osteoporotic elderly women — sacral insufficiency fractures mimic SI joint pain
Be cautious about industry-sponsored SI fusion studies — over 20 companies now compete in this space
Most patients confirmed with SI joint pain do not want fusion — they need to be quite debilitated to proceed
